article.overview: A penetrometer is an instrument that measures how much force is needed to push a probe into soil or regolith, and how the resistance changes with depth. On the Moon, penetrometers are used to estimate the mechanical strength of the regolith, the loose layer of fragmented rock and dust covering the lunar surface. This information matters for landing-site engineering, excavation, construction and the design of surface hardware. Some penetrometer designs are also being explored for detecting water ice in the subsurface. The best-documented flown examples are the Apollo 15 and Apollo 16 Lunar Self-Recording Penetrometers, which astronauts pushed into the surface during extravehicular activity. The Soviet Luna 13 lander also carried a penetrometer, which used a small explosive charge to drive its probe. Newer penetrometer concepts, including percussive designs for low-gravity use, have been tested in laboratory simulants but, as far as the sources reviewed show, have not been confirmed as flown.
article.description: A lunar penetrometer typically consists of a probe or cone, a shaft or drive mechanism, a means of applying or measuring force, and a way of recording depth. The probe is pushed or driven into the soil, and the force and depth data are used to estimate soil properties such as cohesion and friction angle. Some designs record data mechanically, for example on a drum, while others use electronic sensors and telemetry. Penetrometers are simple in concept but demanding in practice. On the Moon, a static push must overcome the soil's resistance using the weight of the operator or the platform. Dry, fine-grained regolith can resist penetration strongly, so an astronaut or a rover may be unable to push a probe deep enough. For this reason, some proposed designs use percussion (repeated hammering) to drive the probe with a small reaction force.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purpose of a lunar penetrometer is geotechnical characterisation, meaning the measurement of soil properties relevant to engineering. The Apollo 15 and 16 experiments were designed to measure the lunar soil's mechanical properties at the surface and at depth, to examine how those properties vary across a site, and to help interpret other surface experiments. The Apollo 16 documentation also describes the aim of developing lunar surface models for future engineering work. Potential applications include: estimating bearing strength for landers, habitats and other surface structures; assessing whether regolith can be excavated, compacted or used as a construction material; supporting trafficability studies for rovers and astronauts; detecting water ice in the subsurface, which is the stated goal of the percussive designs discussed below; and calibrating and validating lunar soil models and simulants.
article.operating_principle: In the Apollo penetrometers, the astronaut pushed on the upper end of the instrument, driving a bearing plate or interchangeable cone into the soil. A reference pad rested on the surface and provided a fixed datum for depth. Force was measured by the deflection of a calibrated coil spring, which rotated a recording drum in proportion to the applied force. Depth was recorded by a stylus driven by a cable from the reference pad. Because the record was mechanical, no electronics were needed to capture the data. The drum was returned to Earth, and the investigators read the etched traces and transferred them to charts. The Apollo documentation explains that soil strength can be inferred from the penetration record using soil-mechanics theory. The method combines the measured force-depth relationship with assumptions about the failure surface of the soil and the friction between the probe and the soil. The inferred values depend strongly on these assumptions. In percussive penetrometers, a hammering mechanism delivers repeated impacts to the probe. The impacts reduce the static force needed from the platform, which the laboratory study describes as useful in low gravity. Penetration rate is then used as an indicator of ice content.
article.scientific_importance: Penetrometer measurements give direct, in-situ information about regolith strength. Orbital imaging and remote sensing cannot provide this information, and sample return alone cannot show how strength changes with depth at a given location. The Apollo penetrometer data therefore contributed to early understanding of lunar soil mechanics, which in turn informed later thinking about surface operations and engineering. Penetrometer data are also important for models of the Moon's regolith. The Apollo 16 documentation notes that its method was tested on dense, fine sandy soils and used friction data from a ground-basalt lunar simulant rather than lunar soil itself. Future measurements in different terrains, including the polar regions where water ice may be present, would extend this record. The NGI press release describing an ESA-sponsored calibration chamber notes that there is little in-situ data for the lunar poles.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a penetrometer. Different missions and proposals have used different probe shapes, force ranges, depth capabilities and recording systems. The examples below describe specific instruments and should not be treated as typical values for all penetrometers. Where a value is not published in the sources reviewed, it is marked as not stated (null).

examples.name: Apollo 15 and 16 Lunar Self-Recording Penetrometer (LSRP / SRP)
examples.flight_status: Flown on Apollo 15 and Apollo 16. NASA PDS refers to both as LSRP; the Apollo 16 report uses the name Self Recording Penetrometer (SRP).
examples.mass_note: 2.3 kg is the Apollo 15 LSRP value given in the PDS instrument document. The Apollo 16 mass is not stated in the sources reviewed.

max_penetration_force_n.note: The two sources give different maximum force values. The reason is not explained in the sources reviewed.

examples.sensor_configuration: No electronic sensors described. Force is measured by deflection of a calibrated coil spring, which rotates a recording drum (a 30 degree rotation at maximum force, per the PDS document). Depth is recorded by a stylus driven by a cable from the reference pad.
examples.power: Not stated for the penetrometer. The PDS document mentions a battery only for the separate lunar surface drill.
examples.museum_object_dimensions_note: Smithsonian NASM object A19750056000 lists 3-D dimensions of 38.1 x 8.9 x 106.7 cm. The object is described as used for training, so this is not confirmed as the flight unit size.
examples.construction: Aluminium, plastic, synthetic fabric and Velcro, according to the NASM object record for the training unit.
examples.deployment: Hand-deployed by astronauts during extravehicular activity. The astronaut pushed the upper end through an extension handle while the reference pad stayed on the surface as the depth datum. The reference pad folds for storage, the astronaut advanced an index register between runs, and the instrument head was stowed for return after testing.
examples.known_problems: On Apollo 15, the reference pad could ride up the shaft slightly if the instrument was vibrated after positioning, because the friction between the pad and shaft was lower than expected. The PDS document says this had a small effect on the readings.
examples.analysis_method: Soil strength (cohesion and friction angle) is derived from the penetration record using soil-mechanics theory. One friction ratio input (delta/phi = 0.5) came from tests with a ground-basalt lunar simulant. The Apollo 16 documentation states that one penetration cannot uniquely determine both cohesion and friction angle.

examples.name: Luna 13 penetrometer
examples.type: Flown Soviet lunar lander instrument (Luna 13, December 1966)
examples.flight_status: Flown. The penetrometer was one of two instruments on a spring-loaded boom; the other boom carried a backscatter densitometer.
examples.mechanism: Penetrating force supplied by a minute explosive charge, according to a Wikipedia summary of Luna 13.
examples.reported_result: Regolith density of 800 kg/m3 attributed to the penetrometer in the Wikipedia summary. The same article attributes a density inference to the densitometer, and does not explain the overlap. Treat as unverified until primary Soviet mission documentation is checked.
examples.mission_dates: Lander touched down on 24 December 1966; transmissions ended on 28 December 1966 when batteries were exhausted.

examples.name: SAMPLR penetrometer (Sample Acquisition, Morphology Filtering and Probing of Lunar Regolith)
examples.type: Planned robotic lander-mounted penetrometer; flight not confirmed
examples.flight_status: Planned for Masten Mission One (CLPS, planned 2023 launch). Masten filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in July 2022 and was acquired by Astrobotic in September 2022. The sources reviewed do not confirm that the mission or payload flew.
examples.sensing: Published abstract states that penetration rate correlates with ice content. No sensor specifications were found in the sources reviewed.
examples.development: Collaboration between Maxar, NASA Goddard Spaceflight Center and the Colorado School of Mines Center for Space Resources, under NASA LSITP.

examples.name: Percussive cone penetrometer laboratory prototype (NASA KSC / Honeybee Robotics, 2016)
examples.type: Ground-tested laboratory prototype; not confirmed as flown
examples.flight_status: Tested in lunar regolith simulant mixed with ice. The paper describes potential use on small platforms in low gravity, but does not state that the device has flown.
examples.down_force_note: Force at which the percussive tool penetrated material that a static cone could not penetrate at full body weight.
examples.penetration_depth_note: Depth to which the tool loosened the simulant and broke up the ice, per the paper abstract.
examples.ice_content_reported: 8 by weight, as printed without a clear unit (most likely percent).
examples.detection_principle: Penetration rate depends on ice content and was largely unaffected by down-force.
examples.limitations_reported: Some icy material may not be penetrable. The probe tip can become stuck and fail to retract.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Dimensions vary widely between instruments. The Apollo LSRP used a long shaft with a 2.54 cm by 12.7 cm bearing plate and interchangeable cones of 1.29 to 6.45 cm2 base area. The overall instrument dimensions were not stated in the PDS text for the flight unit. A museum training unit of the Apollo instrument is recorded at 38.1 x 8.9 x 106.7 cm, but this is not confirmed as the flight configuration. Dimensions of the Luna 13, SAMPLR and percussive laboratory designs are not stated in the sources reviewed. A new penetrometer's dimensions would depend on its intended depth, force range and mounting constraints.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The only penetrometer mass value confirmed in the sources reviewed is 2.3 kg for the Apollo 15 LSRP (PDS instrument document). The Apollo 16 SRP mass, and the masses of the Luna 13, SAMPLR and percussive laboratory designs, are not stated. Mass matters for launch and lander capacity. For a surface penetrometer, the reaction force the platform must supply is also important. The percussive laboratory work states that its design needs less down-force than a static cone, which the authors describe as useful for low-gravity platforms.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A penetrometer used on the Moon must operate in vacuum, with large day-night temperature variations and abrasive dust. Mechanical parts and recording systems must tolerate these conditions, and any electronics need thermal protection. For the Apollo instruments, which were operated by astronauts during extravehicular activity, the operating environment included the practical limits of surface EVA, such as handling, stowage and the time available for each measurement. Measurement quality also depends on the stability of the reference datum. On Apollo 15, the reference pad could move slightly up the shaft if the instrument was vibrated after positioning, and the PDS documentation says this had a small effect on the readings. Percussive and robotic designs need to manage the reaction forces they apply to the platform and the risk of the probe sticking. Calibration is an important requirement. An ESA-sponsored project led by the Norwegian Geotechnical Institute, announced in June 2025, is designing a cone penetration calibration chamber intended to test instruments in lunar vacuum and temperature conditions. The NGI page does not state the chamber's dimensions, vacuum level or temperature range, and describes the chamber as designed rather than built.
article.limitations: The Apollo penetrometers can measure only to a limited depth. The Apollo 15 and 16 instruments reached a maximum of 76 cm, and the force ceiling was 111 N or 215 N depending on the document. Measurements are limited to the soil types and locations tested. The interpretation of results depends on several assumptions. The Apollo 16 documentation states that one penetration cannot uniquely determine both cohesion and friction angle, because more than one combination of values fits the same measurement. The failure-surface model was tested on dense, fine sandy soils, and the friction ratio was taken from tests with a ground-basalt simulant rather than lunar soil. For ice detection, the 2016 laboratory work shows a relationship between penetration rate and ice content in simulant, but it does not establish performance in natural lunar regolith. The paper also warns that some icy material may not be penetrable and that the probe tip can become stuck and fail to retract.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: Penetrometers have been delivered to the Moon as hand-carried astronaut tools (Apollo) and are proposed as robotic arm-mounted or lander-mounted instruments (SAMPLR) or as small rover or lander payloads (percussive laboratory concept). No verified interface specifications for a named lander or rover were obtained in this research.
transportation_process: Integrate the instrument into the spacecraft or lander payload compartment on Earth, or stow it as a hand tool for astronaut carriage.
Launch and transfer to the Moon on the mission's transport vehicle.
Deliver to the lunar surface by lander, or by astronaut carriage during an EVA.
Deploy the probe by hand (Apollo), by robotic arm (SAMPLR concept), or by a self-contained percussive mechanism (laboratory concept).
Use a stable reference or mounting point so that depth and force measurements are not disturbed.
Connect any electronics to power and data systems, and protect the probe mechanism from dust and thermal extremes.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Apollo 15 and 16: astronaut-operated, with the astronaut pushing the upper end through an extension handle while the reference pad stayed on the surface. Index register advanced manually between runs. The PDS instrument context pages label the Apollo 15 unit as an LM (lunar module) instrument, which suggests lunar module association, but the stowage arrangement and transport interfaces were not verified in the sources reviewed. SAMPLR concept: robotic arm on a lander-mounted suite. Percussive laboratory concept: a hammering mechanism intended to reduce the static reaction force required from a small rover or lander.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Apollo 15 (1971) and Apollo 16 (1972) carried the self-recording penetrometer for surface soil mechanics experiments. Luna 13 (1966) carried a penetrometer on a spring-loaded boom with an explosive-charge penetration mechanism. The SAMPLR penetrometer was planned for Masten Mission One, which was not confirmed to have flown.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: Compatibility with any specific lander or rover has not been verified. A penetrometer's suitability for a given vehicle would depend on its mass, dimensions, mounting loads, the reaction forces it applies, power demand, data interface and deployment method. The SAMPLR and percussive designs were described by their developers as suitable for lander-mounted or small-platform use, but no verified interface specifications were found, so no lander compatibility is asserted here.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo 15 and 16 penetrometers were among the first systematic in-situ measurements of lunar soil strength carried out by astronauts, and their data form part of the foundation of lunar soil mechanics. The Luna 13 penetrometer is an early example of a robotic penetration measurement on the Moon, although its reported results are less certain. The more recent SAMPLR and percussive designs show continuing interest in penetrometers for ice detection and geotechnical work, but these remain at the planning or laboratory stage in the sources reviewed.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: Apollo force range: the Apollo 15 PDS document gives 111 N as the maximum recordable force, while the Apollo 16 page gives 215 N. The reason for the difference was not established [1][2]. Apollo 16 physical data: mass, overall dimensions and crew procedures for the Apollo 16 SRP were not stated in the sources reviewed. Apollo 16 run count: the dataset summary lists ten runs on 22 April 1972, while a separate Apollo 16 document is cited as recording eleven tests in the second EVA; the count should be checked against primary data. Luna 13 density figure (800 kg/m3) is attributed to the penetrometer in a secondary source and is not verified. SAMPLR flight status: no source confirmed that the SAMPLR penetrometer flew. Percussive ice-content figure: the unit in the 2016 paper is not printed clearly, and the detection threshold should be checked against the original paper. Image assets: no verified direct image asset URL was recorded. Lander compatibility: no verified interface specifications for any named lander were obtained.

The one image object has image_url null because the NASM direct asset links depend on query parameters. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery.

data_quality_notes: Apollo force range conflict: the Apollo 15 PDS document gives 111 N maximum recordable force; the Apollo 16 SRP page gives 215 N. Both are recorded with their sources.
Luna 13 density (800 kg/m3) is attributed to the penetrometer in a Wikipedia summary, which also attributes a density inference to the densitometer. Unverified.
SAMPLR flight status not confirmed. Masten Mission One is described as planned; no source confirms launch or payload outcome.
The 2016 percussive paper reports ice content as '8 by weight' without a printed unit. The unit is presumed to be percent but is not confirmed.

The Michigan Technological University percussive hot cone penetrometer is a different instrument from SAMPLR and from the NASA 2016 percussive prototype. It is mentioned in the article but not included as a separate example.
The ESA-sponsored NGI cone penetration calibration chamber is a ground test facility, not a penetrometer payload. It is described in the environmental section and not as an example.
A search result contained text addressed to an AI assistant asking for a summary of Masten Mission One. This was ignored and is not reflected in the article.
Apollo 16 run count differs between sources (ten runs in the dataset summary; eleven tests cited in a separate Apollo 16 document). Not resolved.
No verified direct image asset URL was obtained. The NASM image is a linked source-page reference.
